name: The Colosseum
blurb: c. 70–80 AD · Arena flooded for staged sea battles at first; underground chambers to hoist gladiators came later
source: Wikimedia Commons: Rome Colosseum exterior 2.jpg

name: The Creation of Adam
blurb: Michelangelo, c. 1512 · a physician argued the drapery around God traces a human brain, down to the brain stem
source: Wikimedia Commons: Michelangelo - Creation of Adam (cropped).jpg

name: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
blurb: Katsushika Hokusai, c. 1831 · made possible by Prussian blue, an imported pigment that didn't fade like Japan's traditional dyes
source: Wikimedia Commons: Great Wave off Kanagawa2.jpg

name: David
blurb: Michelangelo, 1501–1504 · carved from a marble block nicknamed 'the Giant' — two earlier sculptors had already tried and abandoned it
source: Wikimedia Commons: 'David' by Michelangelo JBU0001.JPG

name: Mona Lisa
blurb: Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1503–1519 · Leonardo never delivered her — kept reworking it till he died; Napoleon later hung it in his bedroom
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mona Lisa, by Leonardo da Vinci, from C2RMF natural color.jpg

name: Sistine Chapel Ceiling
blurb: Michelangelo, 1508–1512 · he didn't paint lying down — stood on a scaffold bent backwards for years, paint dripping into his beard
source: Wikimedia Commons: CAPPELLA SISTINA Ceiling.jpg

name: The Starry Night
blurb: Vincent van Gogh, 1889 · painted from van Gogh's asylum; the village below was invented, not visible from his window
source: Wikimedia Commons: Van Gogh - Starry Night - Google Art Project.jpg

name: Stonehenge
blurb: c. 3000–1500 BC · Its smaller 'bluestones' were hauled roughly 150 miles from Wales — how, and by what route, still disputed
source: Wikimedia Commons: Stonehenge2007 07 30.jpg

name: Taj Mahal
blurb: Marble mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal (1653) · its four minarets lean slightly outward — deliberately, so an earthquake would drop them away from the tomb
attribution: Dhirad, picture edited by J. A. Knudsen
source: Wikimedia Commons: Taj Mahal in March 2004.jpg

name: Terracotta Army
blurb: c. 210–209 BC · Discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well; the buried army numbers over 8,000, no two faces quite alike
source: Wikimedia Commons: Terracota warrior close-up.jpg

name: The Scream
blurb: Edvard Munch, 1893 · Munch's inscription says the figure isn't screaming, but covering its ears against a scream in nature
source: Wikimedia Commons: Edvard Munch, 1893, The Scream, oil, tempera and pastel on cardboard.jpg

name: Mask of Tutankhamun
blurb: Burial mask of Tutankhamun, c. 1323 BC · in 2014, museum staff snapped off the braided beard while cleaning the case, then glued it back on with epoxy
source: Wikimedia Commons: Tutanchamun Maske.jpg

name: Venus de Milo
blurb: c. 150–125 BC · Found in 1820 by a farmer digging a field on Milos — already armless, the cause lost to history
source: Wikimedia Commons: Venus de Milo Louvre Ma399 n4.jpg

name: American Gothic
blurb: Grant Wood, 1930 · the stern pair aren't married — Wood's models were his sister and his dentist, posed separately, never meeting
source: Wikimedia Commons: Grant DeVolson Wood - American Gothic.jpg

name: Big Ben
blurb: Clock tower of the Palace of Westminster (1859) · Big Ben is technically just the bell — the tower itself wasn't officially named Elizabeth Tower until 2012
source: Wikimedia Commons: Big Ben Elizabeth Tower London 2023 01.jpg

name: The Birth of Venus
blurb: Sandro Botticelli, c. 1484–1486 · the face is traditionally Simonetta Vespucci, Florence's celebrated beauty — painted years after she died
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sandro Botticelli - La nascita di Venere - Google Art Project - edited.jpg

name: Bust of Nefertiti
blurb: c. 1345 BC · Only one eye was ever inlaid — the left is a bare socket, perhaps left deliberately as a sculptor's model
source: Wikimedia Commons: Nofretete Neues Museum.jpg

name: Chichén Itzá
blurb: El Castillo, the Temple of Kukulcán (8th–12th century) · twice a year, at the equinoxes, sunlight and shadow on its steps form a serpent slithering down the pyramid
source: Wikimedia Commons: Chichen Itza 3.jpg

name: Christ the Redeemer
blurb: Art Deco colossus above Rio de Janeiro, completed 1931 · struck by lightning more than once — a 2014 bolt chipped a thumb and finger, repaired in soapstone weeks later
source: Wikimedia Commons: Christ the Redeemer - Cristo Redentor.jpg

name: Easter Island Moai
blurb: c. 1250–1500 AD · Many of the famous 'heads' have full bodies — buried to the shoulders by centuries of soil
source: Wikimedia Commons: Moai Rano raraku.jpg

name: Eiffel Tower
blurb: Gustave Eiffel's iron tower (1889) · built as a temporary exhibit meant to come down after 20 years — it survived as an excellent radio antenna
source: Wikimedia Commons: Eiffel Tower Paris June 2010.jpg

name: Fushimi Inari
blurb: Kyoto's mountain tunnel of thousands of vermilion torii gates · each gate was privately donated by a business hoping for prosperity — donor's name and date on the back
source: Wikimedia Commons: Torii path with lantern at Fushimi Inari Taisha Shrine, Kyoto, Japan.jpg

name: Cappadocia
blurb: Turkey's valley of volcanic 'fairy chimneys' and rock-cut cave dwellings
source: Wikimedia Commons: Göreme Valley in Cappadocia edit1.jpg

name: Great Pyramid of Giza
blurb: Tomb of Pharaoh Khufu (c. 2560 BC) · the tallest human-made structure on Earth for almost 3,800 years — until Lincoln Cathedral's spire, c. 1311
source: Wikimedia Commons: Spelterini Pyramids.jpg

name: Great Sphinx of Giza
blurb: Limestone guardian with a lion's body (c. 2500 BC) · its missing nose is blamed on Napoleon — but sketches predating his birth already show it gone
source: Wikimedia Commons: Great Sphinx (أبو الهول).jpg

name: Hagia Sophia
blurb: Byzantine cathedral, later mosque (537 AD) · a Viking guardsman scratched 'Halfdan' into the upstairs balustrade over a thousand years ago — still legible
source: Wikimedia Commons: Hagia Sophia Mars 2013.jpg

name: Kremlin Walls
blurb: Fortified citadel walls and towers, mainly 15th century · its swallow-tail battlements were designed by imported Italian architects, echoing Milan's Sforza Castle
source: Wikimedia Commons: Moscow Kremlin Towers of south wall.jpg

name: The Last Supper
blurb: Leonardo da Vinci, c. 1495–1498 · Leonardo used an experimental technique instead of true fresco — it began flaking within his own lifetime
source: Wikimedia Commons: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) - The Last Supper (1495-1498).jpg

name: Leaning Tower of Pisa
blurb: Bell tower two centuries in the building (1173–1372) — leaning before it was even finished · Italy
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Duomo and Tower of Pisa at sunrise.jpg

name: Lycurgus Cup
blurb: Roman dichroic glass cage-cup that changes colour in light, 4th century AD · British Museum, London
source: Wikimedia Commons: Front of 4th century CE Roman Lycurgus Cup, British Museum (1958,1202.1).jpg

name: Machu Picchu
blurb: Inca citadel in the Andes (c. 1450) · never found by the Spanish — stayed unknown until a local farmer led an American historian there in 1911
source: Wikimedia Commons: Machu Picchu with Huayna Picchu Pérou (3).jpg

name: Neuschwanstein Castle
blurb: Ludwig II’s fairy-tale castle (1869–1886) — he died before it was finished · Bavaria, Germany
source: Wikimedia Commons: Neuschwanstein Castle 2024-02.jpg

name: Notre-Dame de Paris
blurb: Gothic cathedral of Paris (1163–1345) · its roof and spire burned in a catastrophic 2019 fire — the rebuilt cathedral reopened in December 2024
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Paris, 20 March 2014.jpg

name: Pamukkale
blurb: Turkey's cascading white travertine terraces and turquoise thermal pools · its name means 'cotton castle,' after the white mineral crust — Romans built the spa city Hierapolis on top
source: Wikimedia Commons: TR Pamukkale White Terraces asv2020-02 img16.jpg

name: The Parthenon
blurb: Temple of Athena on the Acropolis (438 BC) · it stood nearly 2,000 years intact — until a 1687 mortar shell hit gunpowder stored inside by the Ottomans
source: Wikimedia Commons: Attica 06-13 Athens 50 View from Philopappos - Acropolis Hill.jpg

name: Pena Palace
blurb: Portugal's flamboyant Romanticist palace crowning the hills of Sintra, 19th century · its architect mashed Gothic, Moorish, Renaissance and Manueline styles onto one building, on a whim
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sintra Portugal Palácio da Pena-01.jpg

name: Petra
blurb: Al-Khazneh, the Treasury carved in rock (1st century AD) · its facade urn is pockmarked with bullet holes — Bedouin believed treasure was hidden inside and shot at it
attribution:
Al_Khazneh_Petra.jpg: Graham Racher from London, UK
derivative work: MrPanyGoff
source: Wikimedia Commons: Al Khazneh Petra edit 2.jpg

name: Red Square
blurb: Named “Krasnaya” (beautiful/red) in the 17th century, cobbled in 1804 · Moscow, Russia
source: Wikimedia Commons: Red Square in Moscow (general view in 2025).jpg

name: Saint Basil's Cathedral
blurb: Ivan the Terrible's many-coloured cathedral (1561) · legend says Ivan the Terrible blinded its architect so he'd never top it — almost certainly false
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sant Vasily cathedral in Moscow.JPG

name: Sunflowers
blurb: Vincent van Gogh, 1888 · painted for the guest bedroom of the Yellow House in Arles, while van Gogh awaited his friend Paul Gauguin
source: Wikimedia Commons: Vincent van Gogh - Sunflowers - VGM F458.jpg

name: The Thinker
blurb: Auguste Rodin, 1904 · originally titled 'The Poet' — conceived as Dante brooding over Hell atop Rodin's unfinished Gates of Hell
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Thinker, Auguste Rodin.jpg

name: Tower Bridge
blurb: London’s 1894 bascule bridge — the one everyone calls London Bridge (that’s the plain one upstream)
source: Wikimedia Commons: Tower Bridge London Dusk Feb 2006.jpg

name: Trevi Fountain
blurb: Rome's Baroque wishing fountain, completed 1762 · tourists toss over a million euros in every year — Rome sweeps the coins out nightly for a Catholic charity
source: Wikimedia Commons: Fuente de Trevi, Roma, Italia, 2022-09-15, DD 02.jpg

name: Abu Simbel
blurb: Ramesses II's rock-cut colossi guarding Nubia — sliced into 1,000+ blocks and reassembled 65 metres higher in a spectacular 1960s UNESCO rescue from the rising Aswan Dam waters, 13th century BC.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Templo de Ramsés II, Abu Simbel, Egipto, 2022-04-02, DD 03.jpg

name: Acropolis of Athens
blurb: Citadel with the Parthenon (5th century BC) · in 1941, two Greek teenagers scaled the rock by night and tore down the Nazi flag — an early act of resistance
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Acropolis of Athens from Philopappos Hill on June 16, 2020.jpg

name: Angkor Wat
blurb: Khmer temple complex (12th century) · It's today the only building on any national flag — Cambodia's
source: Wikimedia Commons: 20171128 Angkor Wat 5562 DxO.jpg

name: Antikythera Mechanism
blurb: Ancient Greek astronomical computer (2nd century BC) · pulled from a 1901 shipwreck by sponge divers; not recognised as a computer until X-rays, decades on
source: Wikimedia Commons: Antikythera Mechanism - National Archaeological Museum, Athens by Joy of Museum.jpg

name: Aztec Sun Stone
blurb: 24-tonne carved calendar stone, c. 1502–1520 (reign of Moctezuma II) · despite the name, it likely wasn't a calendar — more likely an altar, dug up by accident in 1790
source: Wikimedia Commons: Aztec Sun Stone or Calendar Stone.jpg

name: Bayeux Tapestry
blurb: 70 metres of embroidered Norman Conquest, c. 1070s · technically embroidery, not tapestry — its border shows Halley's Comet as an omen before Hastings
source: Wikimedia Commons: Bayeux Tapestry scene57 Harold death.jpg

name: Bran Castle
blurb: Transylvanian clifftop castle popularly tied to Dracula, 14th century · Bram Stoker never set foot in Romania, likely never saw this castle — the Dracula link is a tourism invention
source: Wikimedia Commons: Bran Castle TB1.jpg

name: Brandenburg Gate
blurb: Neoclassical gate topped by the Quadriga (1791) · Napoleon carted its bronze Quadriga to Paris as war booty in 1806; Prussians brought it home in 1814
source: Wikimedia Commons: Brandenburger Tor abends.jpg

name: Carcassonne
blurb: France's great walled medieval fortress-city, famously restored by Viollet-le-Duc · its fairy-tale pointed roofs are 19th-century — restorer Viollet-le-Duc borrowed the look from northern France
source: Wikimedia Commons: Outer walls of the fortified city of Carcassonne 2.jpg

name: Charles Bridge
blurb: Gothic bridge of 1357, lined with Baroque saints added from 1683 · legend holds egg yolks were mixed into the mortar — one town supposedly sent hard-boiled eggs by mistake
source: Wikimedia Commons: Prague Charles Bridge 2021 30.jpg

name: Codex Gigas
blurb: Giant medieval manuscript known as the 'Devil's Bible' for its full-page devil portrait, 13th century · National Library of Sweden
source: Wikimedia Commons: Codex-Gigas-Devil-enhanced.jpg

name: Doge's Palace
blurb: Venetian Gothic seat of government, mainly 14th-15th century · connected to the prison by the Bridge of Sighs — Casanova was held there, and pulled off a famous jail escape
source: Wikimedia Commons: Doge's Palace Venice sea facade.jpg

name: Dome of the Rock
blurb: Islamic shrine with a golden dome (691 AD) · Jerusalem
source: Wikimedia Commons: Jerusalem-2013-Temple Mount-Dome of the Rock & Chain 02.jpg

name: Kailasa Temple
blurb: Colossal temple carved top-down from a single Indian cliff, 8th century AD
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Kailash Temple (also Kailasanatha),Cave No.16.jpg

name: Florence Cathedral Dome
blurb: Brunelleschi's self-supporting dome, completed 1436 · Brunelleschi built it with no scaffolding, inventing new hoisting machines to pull it off
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cupola di santa maria del fiore dal campanile di giotto, 01.JPG

name: Girl with a Pearl Earring
variants: la jeune fille à la perle
the girl with the pearl earring
blurb: Johannes Vermeer, c. 1665 · not a real person but a 'tronie,' an imagined study — the 'pearl' is probably glass, too large to be real
source: Wikimedia Commons: Girl with a Pearl Earring.jpg

name: Göbekli Tepe
blurb: The world's oldest known temple, in Anatolia, c. 9500 BC · predates Stonehenge by 6,000 years and farming itself — builders later buried the site, reasons debated
source: Wikimedia Commons: Göbekli Tepe site (1).JPG

name: Golden Gate Bridge
blurb: Art Deco suspension bridge (1937) · its orange nearly became black-and-yellow, the Navy's pick — its architect fought for International Orange
source: Wikimedia Commons: Golden Gate Bridge, north tower detail.jpg

name: The Golden Pavilion
blurb: Zen temple covered in gold leaf (1397, rebuilt 1955) · today's building is a 1955 replica — a monk burned the original down in 1950, inspiring Mishima's novel
source: Wikimedia Commons: Water reflection of Kinkaku-ji Temple a sunny day, Kyoto, Japan.jpg

name: Golden Temple
blurb: Sikhism's holiest shrine, gilded and mirrored in its sacred pool at Amritsar — its free kitchen (langar) feeds over 100,000 visitors a day, no questions asked.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, India.jpg

name: Great Mosque of Córdoba
blurb: Striped double arches of the Mezquita (8th–10th century) · Charles V reportedly regretted the cathedral built inside it, saying they'd ruined something unique
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mezquita cordoba arcos flotantes.jpg

name: Great Wall of China
blurb: Fortifications spanning northern China (7th century BC – 17th century AD) · contrary to myth, it isn't visible from space unaided — astronauts from Apollo to the ISS confirm it
source: Wikimedia Commons: 20090529 Great Wall 8185.jpg

name: Ishtar Gate
blurb: Glazed-brick gate of Babylon (c. 575 BC) · Berlin's gate is rebuilt from excavated original bricks — Iraq built its own replica at the real site
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pergamon museum Ishtar Gate.jpg

name: Itsukushima Shrine
blurb: Japan's vermilion torii gate that floats at high tide, off Miyajima · The great vermilion gate isn't anchored to the seabed at all — it stands upright purely under its own weight
source: Wikimedia Commons: Miyajima Itsukushima shrine floating tori gate.jpg

name: Knossos Palace
blurb: Minoan Bronze Age palace complex with griffin frescoes, c. 1700 BC · much of it is a controversial concrete rebuild by excavator Arthur Evans — critics call it his imagination
source: Wikimedia Commons: Knossos Throne-room 20230604 110755.jpg

name: Konark Sun Temple
blurb: Odisha's 13th-century temple built as the sun god's stone chariot · its 24 carved stone wheels aren't decoration — each works as a sundial, telling time by its shadow
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sun Temple Main Structure, Konark, Orissa.jpg

name: Lalibela
blurb: Ethiopia's cross-shaped church hewn down into living rock, 12th–13th century · legend says angels carved by night, after the king survived poisoning and dreamed of a new Jerusalem
source: Wikimedia Commons: Bete Giyorgis 01.jpg

name: Liberty Bell
blurb: Cast 1752, cracked on its first test ring and recast in 1753 · Liberty Bell Center, Philadelphia
source: Wikimedia Commons: Liberty Bell 2008.jpg

name: Liberty Leading the People
blurb: Eugène Delacroix, 1830 · Delacroix didn't fight in 1830 — he told his brother he'd paint for his country instead
source: Wikimedia Commons: Eugène Delacroix - La liberté guidant le peuple.jpg

name: Mask of Agamemnon
blurb: Schliemann cabled the King of Greece 'I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon' when he found it in 1876 — except it predates the Trojan War by roughly 300 years, so it isn't Agamemnon's face at all.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Agamemnon mask NAMA Athens Greece.jpg

name: Meenakshi Temple
blurb: Madurai's Hindu temple crowned by towering, thousand-figured painted gopurams · its towering gopurams carry an estimated 33,000 painted sculptures, repainted every twelve years in a festival
source: Wikimedia Commons: Meenakshi Temple, Gopuram, Madurai, India.jpg

name: Milan Cathedral
blurb: Gothic cathedral with 135 spires, begun 1386 · nearly six centuries in the making — not officially finished until 1965, with a last set of bronze doors
source: Wikimedia Commons: Milan Cathedral from Piazza del Duomo.jpg

name: Mont-Saint-Michel
blurb: Abbey rising from a tidal island (8th–16th century) · local legend says the tide comes in 'at the speed of a galloping horse' — among the fastest in Europe
source: Wikimedia Commons: 00 0572 Mont Saint Michel abbey.jpg

name: Moray
blurb: Inca concentric agricultural terraces sunk into the Peruvian highlands · temperatures differ by up to 15°C between top and bottom terraces — likely an Inca crop-testing lab
source: Wikimedia Commons: Moray, Peru - Laslovarga (6).jpg

name: Stari Most
blurb: Ottoman single-arch bridge over the Neretva at Mostar, rebuilt after the 1990s war · local divers still leap from its parapet into the river, a rite of passage now an annual competition
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mostar Old Town Panorama 2007.jpg

name: Mount Nemrut
blurb: Colossal toppled god-heads crowning a royal Anatolian tomb-mountain, 1st century BC · a minor king carved himself among the gods at colossal scale — the heads toppled later, likely from quakes
source: Wikimedia Commons: Giant Statues of Commagene Kingdom.jpg

name: Mount Rushmore
blurb: Four presidents carved in granite (1927–1941) · the sculptor planned to carve the presidents to their waists — funding ran out in 1941, leaving just the heads
source: Wikimedia Commons: Dean Franklin - 06.04.03 Mount Rushmore Monument (by-sa).jpg

name: Peterhof Palace
blurb: Imperial palace and fountain gardens, founded 1714 · its fountains run purely on gravity, fed by reservoirs through kilometres of canals — no pumps, ever
source: Wikimedia Commons: 00 2989 Sampson Fountain - Peterhof, Russia.jpg

name: Michelangelo's Pietà
blurb: Mary cradling the dead Christ (1499) · St. Peter's Basilica, Vatican
source: Wikimedia Commons: Michelangelo's Pieta 5450 cropncleaned edit.jpg

name: Pont du Gard Aqueduct
blurb: Three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge, 1st century AD · the channel drops just 2.5cm per 100 metres over its 50km run — precise enough for gravity alone
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pont du Gard (30).jpg

name: Prague Castle
blurb: Hilltop castle complex with St Vitus Cathedral, founded 9th century · twice, disputes were settled by throwing officials out the window — the 1618 one sparked the Thirty Years' War
source: Wikimedia Commons: Castillo de Praga, Praga, República Checa, 2022-07-02, DD 209.jpg (cropped to the cathedral and palace)

name: Predjama Castle
blurb: Renaissance castle built into the mouth of a cliff cave in Slovenia — where, according to legend, the outlaw knight Erazem was killed by a cannonball while using the privy, the one weak point in an otherwise impregnable fortress.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Predjama Castle, Slovenia, 20240502 0833 7417.jpg

name: Rialto Bridge
blurb: Stone bridge over the Grand Canal, completed 1591 · Michelangelo and Palladio both had designs rejected — critics predicted the arch built would collapse
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ponte di Rialto Venice 1.jpg

name: Sagrada Família
blurb: Gaudí's unfinished basilica (begun 1882) · its central tower was finished in Feb 2026, a century after Gaudí died — now the tallest church on Earth
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sagrada Familia March 2015-14a.jpg

name: Sigiriya
blurb: Sri Lanka's palace-fortress atop a sheer volcanic plug, 5th century AD · visitors have scrawled poems on its polished 'Mirror Wall' for a thousand years, many about painted maidens
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Sigiriya Rock Fortress.jpg

name: St Mark's Basilica
blurb: Venice's golden Byzantine basilica on the Piazza San Marco · Venetian merchants reportedly smuggled St Mark's relics from Alexandria hidden under pork, past customs
source: Wikimedia Commons: Facade of St. Mark's Basilica-Venice.jpg

name: Statue of Liberty
blurb: Liberty Enlightening the World (1886) · its sculptor first pitched a torch-bearing woman as a Suez lighthouse — Egypt balked, so he recycled it
source: Wikimedia Commons: Statue of Liberty frontal 2.jpg

name: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
variants: a sunday on la grande jatte
sunday afternoon on the island of la grande jatte
blurb: Georges Seurat, 1884–1886 · made of tiny dots of pure colour, meant to blend in the viewer's eye, not on the canvas — years in the making
source: Wikimedia Commons: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, Georges Seurat, 1884.jpg

name: Sutton Hoo Helmet
blurb: c. 625 AD · British Museum, London — found in a ship burial in a Suffolk field in 1939, the discovery behind the 2021 Netflix film The Dig.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sutton Hoo helmet reconstructed.jpg

name: Paro Taktsang
blurb: Bhutan's Tiger's Nest monastery clinging to a Himalayan cliff, 17th century · Named for a legend that a guru flew here on the back of a flying tigress to subdue a demon haunting the cliff
source: Wikimedia Commons: Paro Taktsang, Bhutan (edited).jpg

name: Temple of Poseidon
blurb: Doric marble temple on a sea cliff, 5th century BC · Lord Byron carved his own name into one of its marble columns in 1810 — the graffiti is still legible today
source: Wikimedia Commons: Temple of Poseidon perspective at Cape Sounion Greece.jpg

name: Tulum
blurb: Maya walled port perched on cliffs above the Caribbean, 13th century · its original name meant 'dawn' — the cliffs face due east, where the Maya watched the sun rise over the sea
source: Wikimedia Commons: Tulum - God of the Winds Temple 03.JPG

name: Venus of Willendorf
blurb: c. 28,000–25,000 BC · Natural History Museum, Vienna — carved before farming, writing, or the wheel existed, making her one of the oldest known artworks by tens of thousands of years.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Venus von Willendorf 01.jpg

name: Vitruvian Man
blurb: Leonardo da Vinci's study of human proportions (c. 1490) · kept in storage almost permanently, light-sensitive on paper — shown publicly only a few weeks every six years
source: Wikimedia Commons: Da Vinci Vitruve Luc Viatour.jpg

name: Windsor Castle
blurb: The world's oldest inhabited castle, a royal residence west of London since 1070 · a 1992 fire tore through 100-plus rooms — restoration was paid for by opening Buckingham Palace to visitors
source: Wikimedia Commons: Castle View from Alexandra Park - Round Tower, St George's Chapel and the Curfew Tower. Windsor, UK.jpg

name: Winged Victory of Samothrace
blurb: c. 200–190 BC · Discovered shattered on a Greek island in 1863 — a missing hand turned up decades later, never reattached
source: Wikimedia Commons: Nike of Samothrake Louvre Ma2369 n4.jpg

name: Winter Palace
blurb: Baroque imperial palace, completed 1762 · the 1917 'storming' was almost bloodless — the dramatic version is a staged 1920 re-enactment
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Winter Palace and the Alexander Column, Saint Petersburg, Russia.jpg

name: Wright Flyer
blurb: The machine of the first powered flight, Kitty Hawk 1903 · Its first powered flight covered about 120 feet in 12 seconds — shorter than the wingspan of a Boeing 747
source: Wikimedia Commons: First flight3.jpg

name: Alfred Jewel
blurb: Anglo-Saxon gold and enamel aestel inscribed for King Alfred, 9th century AD · found by a farmer ploughing in 1693, near where Alfred hid from Vikings — inscribed 'Alfred ordered me made'
source: Wikimedia Commons: Alfred Jewel Ashmolean 2014.JPG

name: Amber Fort
blurb: Rajput hilltop fort-palace of pale sandstone above Jaipur, 16th–17th century · its Sheesh Mahal, 'Mirror Palace,' is lined with mirrors — one candle makes it glitter like starlight
source: Wikimedia Commons: Amber Fort, Jaipur, 20191219 1045 9589.jpg

name: Arc de Triomphe
blurb: Napoleonic triumphal arch, completed 1836 · beneath it burns an eternal flame, relit by hand nightly since 1923, even under Nazi occupation
source: Wikimedia Commons: Arc Triomphe.jpg

name: Arena of Verona
blurb: Roman amphitheatre still used for opera, 1st century AD · only four arches of its outer wall survive, most fell in a 12th-century quake — it's hosted opera since 1913
source: Wikimedia Commons: Verona Arena 01.jpg

name: Bagan
blurb: Myanmar's plain studded with thousands of Buddhist temples, 11th–13th century · a hasty 1990s restoration, criticised for inauthentic materials, delayed its UNESCO recognition until 2019
source: Wikimedia Commons: Old Bagan, Myanmar, Landscape of ancient Bagan city.jpg

name: Bayon Temple
blurb: Temple of smiling stone faces (late 12th century) · carved with roughly 200 giant smiling faces, thought to merge its king with a compassionate Buddhist deity
source: Wikimedia Commons: Angkor - Bayon - 004 Tower Faces (8581824754).jpg

name: The Blue Mosque
blurb: Ottoman imperial mosque with six minarets (1616) · its six minarets matched Mecca's holiest mosque, a scandal — the sultan paid for a seventh minaret there
source: Wikimedia Commons: Exterior of Sultan Ahmed I Mosque in Istanbul, Turkey 002.jpg

name: Book of Kells
blurb: Illuminated Gospel manuscript (c. 800 AD) · hidden in its decoration is a tiny doodle of a cat chasing a mouse — monks slipped in playful marginalia
source: Wikimedia Commons: KellsFol034rChiRhoMonogram.jpg

name: Borobudur
blurb: World's largest Buddhist temple (9th century) · abandoned and buried under ash and jungle, it was rediscovered in 1814 on Raffles's orders
source: Wikimedia Commons: Borobudur-Temple-Park Indonesia Stupas-of-Borobudur-04.jpg

name: Boudhanath
blurb: One of the world's largest Buddhist stupas, its painted all-seeing eyes watching over Kathmandu.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Boudhanath stupa, Kathmandu 01.jpg

name: Buckingham Palace
blurb: London residence of the British monarch, remodelled 1913 · in 1982, an intruder scaled the wall and sat on the Queen's bed chatting with her, unnoticed
source: Wikimedia Commons: Buckingham Palace east front facade.jpg

name: Catalan Atlas
blurb: Illuminated medieval world map showing Mansa Musa of Mali enthroned, holding a gold nugget to signal he was the richest man alive, 1375 · Bibliothèque nationale de France
source: Wikimedia Commons: 1375 Atlas Catalan, Europe 02.jpg

name: Catherine Palace
blurb: Rococo imperial palace, rebuilt 1752-56 · its famed Amber Room vanished in Nazi looting, never found — today's version is a 2003 replica
source: Wikimedia Commons: 00 5105 Catherine Palace in Pushkin, Russia.jpg

name: Château de Chambord
blurb: France's most flamboyant Loire château, its famous double-helix staircase rumoured to have been sketched by Leonardo da Vinci, begun for François I in 1519.
source: Wikimedia Commons: France Loir-et-Cher Chambord Chateau 01.jpg

name: Charioteer of Delphi
blurb: Serene bronze victor cast for Delphi's sanctuary, 478 BC · it survived only because a rockslide buried it soon after — most ancient bronzes were melted down
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Charioteer of Delphi, 478 BC, AM of Delphi, 201441.jpg

name: Cologne Cathedral
blurb: Germany's soaring Gothic cathedral of twin openwork spires, completed in 1880 · construction stalled 300 years — a medieval crane sat atop the tower so long it became a landmark itself
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cologne Germany Cologne-Cathedral-West-Facade-01.jpg

name: Ctesiphon
blurb: The soaring brick arch of a Persian palace near Baghdad, 6th century AD · its brick vault is still the largest unreinforced arch on Earth, built with no supporting frame
source: Wikimedia Commons: 001125-TaqKasra-Iraq-IMG 7914-2.jpg

name: Delphi Temple
blurb: Sanctuary of the Delphic oracle, 4th century BC · geologists think the oracle's trance came from gases seeping through a fault beneath the temple floor
source: Wikimedia Commons: Delphes, Grèce. Temple d'Apollon. Six colonnes.jpg

name: Edinburgh Castle
blurb: Scotland's royal fortress atop a volcanic crag — besieged more than any other place in Britain, roughly 26 times across 1,100 years.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Edinburgh Castle Rock.jpg

name: Fasil Ghebbi
blurb: Ethiopia's stone castle-citadel at Gondar, nicknamed 'the Camelot of Africa', 17th century. · built with Portuguese, Indian and Jesuit craftsmen, giving it battlements startlingly European
source: Wikimedia Commons: Fasil Ghebbi (6821475763).jpg

name: The Forbidden City
blurb: Chinese imperial palace (1420) · folklore claims 9,999.5 rooms, one short of Heaven's mythical 10,000 — a modern survey counted around 8,700
source: Wikimedia Commons: Beijing China Forbidden-City-03.jpg

name: Great Buddha of Kamakura
blurb: Bronze Amida Buddha (1252) · it once sat inside a temple hall — repeated tsunamis washed the hall away, so for centuries it's sat outdoors
source: Wikimedia Commons: Kamakura Budda Daibutsu front 1885.jpg

name: Great Enclosure Zimbabwe
blurb: Massive dry-stone walled royal enclosure, 11th–15th century AD · colonial officials insisted outsiders built it — archaeology confirmed it was the Shona's ancestors' work
source: Wikimedia Commons: East Wall Great Enclosure (47614139601).jpg

name: Great Mosque of Djenné
blurb: The world's largest mud-brick building, in Mali, rebuilt in 1907 · every year the whole town turns out to re-plaster its mud walls by hand — rain washes some away annually
source: Wikimedia Commons: Great Mosque of Djenné 1.jpg

name: Gundestrup Cauldron
blurb: Ornate Iron Age silver vessel with Celtic mythological reliefs, c. 150–1 BC · found dismantled in a Danish peat bog, styled from far-off origins — likely a ritual offering
source: Wikimedia Commons: Gundestrup cauldron - F.I.4277.jpg

name: Hadrian's Villa
blurb: Emperor Hadrian's retreat with the arched Canopus pool, 2nd century AD · Hadrian filled it with replicas from his travels, plus a canal honouring Antinous, who drowned in the Nile
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Canopus, Hadrian's Villa, Tivoli (14759103250).jpg

name: Code of Hammurabi
blurb: c. 1754 BC · Louvre, Paris — one of the oldest deciphered law codes of real length, and the source of the phrase 'an eye for an eye'.
source: Wikimedia Commons: P1050763 Louvre code Hammurabi face rwk.JPG

name: Himeji Castle
blurb: Japan's grandest samurai-era castle (1609) · nicknamed the White Heron Castle, it survived WWII bombing — one bomb hit it but never exploded
source: Wikimedia Commons: Himeji Castle 0804 1.jpg

name: Imperial State Crown
blurb: 1937 · Tower of London, London — set with over 2,800 diamonds, it's worn by the monarch only a few times a year, most famously at the State Opening of Parliament.
source: Wikimedia Commons: ImperialStateCrown.jpg

name: Karnak
blurb: Egypt's vast temple of Amun and its forest of columns, at Luxor · built by 30-plus pharaohs over 2,000 years — its Great Hypostyle Hall alone packs 134 giant columns
source: Wikimedia Commons: Karnak Temple Great Hypostyle Hall 2014.jpg

name: Lascaux Cave Paintings
blurb: c. 17,000 BC · The real cave has been sealed since 1963 — tourists' breath grew mould on it; today's visit is a replica
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lascaux painting.jpg

name: Leshan Giant Buddha
blurb: The world’s tallest pre-modern stone Buddha, carved into a river cliff, 713–803 AD · a monk carved it hoping the Buddha would calm a river confluence that kept sinking boats
source: Wikimedia Commons: Leshan Giant Buddha, March 2000 04.jpg

name: Lewis Chessmen
blurb: c. 1150–1200 AD · British Museum, London — their bug-eyed, beard-chewing berserker rooks helped inspire the wizard's chess set in the Harry Potter films.
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Warder, Lewis Chessmen, British Museum.jpg

name: Lindisfarne Gospels
blurb: Illuminated Latin gospel book with carpet pages, c. AD 700 · made on Lindisfarne decades before the 793 Viking raid that marks the Viking Age's start
source: Wikimedia Commons: Meister des Book of Lindisfarne 002.jpg

name: Magna Carta
blurb: 1215 AD · Pope Innocent III annulled it within ten weeks — its legend only took hold centuries later
source: Wikimedia Commons: Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106).jpg

name: Meteora
blurb: Greek Orthodox monasteries perched atop sheer rock pinnacles — one doubled as a villain's lair in the Bond film For Your Eyes Only.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Meteora, 09.jpg

name: Mildenhall Treasure
blurb: Roman silver hoard with the Oceanus Great Dish, 4th century AD · ploughed up by a Suffolk farmer in 1942 — owners kept it quiet before its Roman origins were sorted out
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mildenhall Great Dish, Late Roman period, silver - British Museum - DSC01383.jpg

name: Mycenae Lion Gate
blurb: Monumental citadel gateway relief, c. 1250 BC · Homer called Mycenae 'rich in gold' — confirmed when excavators found gold death masks inside this gate
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lions Gate detail.JPG

name: Naqsh-e Rustam
blurb: Cliff carved with the cross-shaped tombs of Persia's Achaemenid kings · a Persian king later added a relief of a Roman emperor kneeling in submission, Rome's worst defeat
source: Wikimedia Commons: Tombs of Achaemenid Kings at Naqsh-e Rustam (4885711726).jpg

name: Nazca Lines
blurb: Giant desert geoglyphs (500 BC – 500 AD) · carved so large they're unrecognisable from the ground, unnoticed until airplanes flew overhead in the 1920s
source: Wikimedia Commons: Líneas de Nazca, Nazca, Perú, 2015-07-29, DD 52.JPG

name: Nebra Sky Disc
blurb: Bronze Age astronomical disc with gold sun, moon and stars, c. 1600 BC · illegally dug up by looters in 1999, recovered two years later in a police sting on the black market
source: Wikimedia Commons: Himmelsscheibe von Nebra - Landesmuseum für Vorgeschichte in Halle - HD.jpg

name: Olmec Colossal Head
blurb: Giant basalt head of an Olmec ruler (1200–400 BC) · each head is thought a real ruler's portrait in a ballgame helmet — hauled miles without wheels
source: Wikimedia Commons: Olmec Colossal Head, San Lorenzo, Veracruz, 1200-600 BC.jpg

name: Oseberg Ship
blurb: A Viking queen's burial ship, interred c. 834, unearthed 1904 · grave robbers found the mound first but missed most treasures — blue clay preserved the wood
source: Wikimedia Commons: Oseberg Ship - Viking Ship Museum (Oslo).jpg

name: Palace of Versailles
blurb: Royal palace expanded under Louis XIV, 17th century · France smuggled Venetian glassmakers out of Italy, breaking a monopoly, to make its Hall of Mirrors
source: Wikimedia Commons: Garden facade of the Palace of Versailles 2.jpg

name: Pantheon Rome
blurb: Former Roman temple, rebuilt c. AD 113–125 · its dome has an open hole at the top — rain falls through onto a marble floor built with drains
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pantheon Rom 1 cropped.jpg

name: Persepolis
blurb: Gateway of the Achaemenid kings' ceremonial capital · Alexander's army burned it down in 330 BC — payback for Athens, or a drunken party, sources disagree
source: Wikimedia Commons: Persepolis – Gate of All Nations 02.jpg

name: Phaistos Disc
blurb: Crete's undeciphered stamped-clay riddle, c. 1700 BC · no one has found a second example of its stamped symbols — some wonder, half-jokingly, if it's a hoax
source: Wikimedia Commons: Phaistos Disc — Side A.jpg

name: Piri Reis Map
blurb: Ottoman gazelle-skin map of the Atlantic coasts that explicitly cites a now-lost map by Christopher Columbus as one of its sources, 1513 · Topkapi Palace Museum, Istanbul
source: Wikimedia Commons: Piri reis world map 01.jpg

name: Pompeii Forum
blurb: Civic square of the buried Roman city, destroyed AD 79 · the eerily lifelike victim casts weren't bodies — plaster poured into voids left in the hardened ash
source: Wikimedia Commons: Forum in Pompeii 2.jpg

name: Ponte Vecchio
blurb: Medieval stone bridge lined with shops, rebuilt 1345 · retreating Nazis destroyed every other Florence bridge in 1944 — this one survived on Hitler's own orders
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ponte Vecchio sobre el río Arno, Florencia, Italia, 2022-09-19, DD 02.jpg

name: Portland Vase
blurb: Roman cameo-glass vase with white figures on cobalt blue, 1st century AD · smashed into some 200 pieces by a drunk visitor at the British Museum in 1845, pieced back together since
source: Wikimedia Commons: Portland Vase BM Gem4036 n1 resized white-balanced white bg.png

name: Potala Palace
blurb: Former palace of the Dalai Lamas (1649) · standing above 3,700 metres, among the highest palaces ever built — workers hauled materials up by hand
source: Wikimedia Commons: Potala Palace, former residence of Dalai Lama, 2006.jpg

name: Registan
blurb: Samarkand's grand plaza framed by three Timurid madrasas, 15th–17th century · one madrasa breaks Islamic tradition — its facade shows tigers chasing deer, faces peeking from suns
source: Wikimedia Commons: Registan square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan.jpg

name: Rila Monastery
blurb: Bulgaria's grandest Orthodox monastery, its striped arcades ringed by mountains · through nearly five centuries of Ottoman rule, the monastery kept Bulgarian language and learning alive
source: Wikimedia Commons: 2016-07-31 Bulgaria, Rila Monastery DSC 9213 DxO.jpg

name: Roman Forum
blurb: Temple of Saturn, rebuilt 4th century AD after a fire (first dedicated 497 BC) · for centuries after Rome fell it was a cow pasture, nicknamed 'Campo Vaccino,' before excavators dug it out
source: Wikimedia Commons: Roman Forum Temple of Saturn.jpg

name: Rosetta Stone
blurb: 196 BC · British Museum, London — the same decree carved three times, in hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek, which is what let Champollion crack hieroglyphs at last.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Rosetta Stone - front face - corrected image.jpg

name: Sacré-Cœur
blurb: The white-domed basilica crowning Montmartre above Paris, completed in 1914 · built as an act of penance after France's 1870-71 defeat and the bloody suppression of the Paris Commune
source: Wikimedia Commons: Basilique du Sacré-Cœur de Montmartre - Paris - GT-01 - 2024.jpg

name: Sacsayhuamán
blurb: Inca citadel of vast interlocking stones above Cusco, 15th century · stones weighing over 100 tonnes fit so tight a knife can't slide between — how the Inca moved them is unclear
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sacsayhuamán, Cusco, Perú, 2015-07-31, DD 05.JPG

name: Schoenbrunn Palace
blurb: Habsburg summer palace, largely rebuilt 1740s-1750s · six-year-old Mozart did perform here in 1762 — his proposal to young Marie Antoinette is unconfirmed legend
source: Wikimedia Commons: Wien - Schloss Schonbrunn.JPG

name: The School of Athens
blurb: Raphael, 1509–1511 · Raphael gave the philosophers contemporaries' faces — Plato resembles Leonardo, Heraclitus, Michelangelo
source: Wikimedia Commons: "The School of Athens" by Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino.jpg

name: Segovia Aqueduct
blurb: Roman Spain's towering double-tier aqueduct of dry-laid granite, c. 100 AD · legend says the Devil built it overnight for a girl's soul — Romans actually built it without mortar
source: Wikimedia Commons: Acueducto de Segovia 01.jpg

name: St Peter's Basilica
blurb: Renaissance basilica, completed 1626 · funding for it, raised partly by selling indulgences, helped push Luther to launch the Reformation
source: Wikimedia Commons: Facade of Saint Peter's Basilica.jpg

name: St Stephen's Cathedral
blurb: Vienna's Gothic cathedral with its dazzling patterned tiled roof · its patterned roof uses 230,000-plus glazed tiles, forming a mosaic of the double-headed Habsburg eagle
source: Wikimedia Commons: Wien - Stephansdom (1).JPG

name: Staffordshire Hoard
blurb: Largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold and silver metalwork, 7th century AD · found in 2009 by an amateur with a metal detector in a Staffordshire field — almost all war-gear
source: Wikimedia Commons: Sheet Gold Plaque, Staffordshire Hoard.jpg

name: Temple of Hatshepsut
blurb: Terraced mortuary temple of a female pharaoh at Deir el-Bahari, 15th century BC · after her death, her images were hacked out and her name chiselled off, erasing a woman who ruled as pharaoh
source: Wikimedia Commons: Temple of Hatshepsut, Deir el-Bahari, Luxor, Egypt.jpg

name: Temple of Heaven
blurb: Imperial altar of prayer for good harvests (1420) · its main hall was built without a single nail — held together purely by interlocking joints and brackets
source: Wikimedia Commons: 20200110 Temple of Heaven-1.jpg

name: Tikal
blurb: Maya temple-pyramid towering over the Guatemalan rainforest, c. 700 AD — its jungle-topped silhouette played the rebel base on Yavin 4 in the original Star Wars.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Temple of the Great Jaguar, Tikal, Petén, Guatemala.jpg

name: Tower of London
blurb: Royal castle founded 1066–1078 · legend holds the kingdom falls if its ravens leave — wings clipped for centuries, just in case
source: Wikimedia Commons: London, Tower of London -- 2016 -- 4791.jpg

name: Uffington White Horse
blurb: Britain's stylised chalk hill-figure above Oxfordshire, cut c. 1000 BC — legend places St George's dragon-slaying on the bare hill just below it.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Aerial View of Uffington White Horse at Harvest Time - geograph.org.uk - 4403449.jpg

name: Wat Arun
blurb: Bangkok's Temple of Dawn and its porcelain-clad spire on the Chao Phraya · its glittering surface is broken Chinese porcelain, repurposed from ships' ballast unloaded in Bangkok's port
source: Wikimedia Commons: WAT ARUN TEMPLE CHAO PRAYA RIVER BANGKOK THAILAND FEB 2012 (6985905427).jpg

name: Westminster Abbey
variants: collegiate church of st peter westminster
blurb: Gothic royal church, mainly 13th–16th century · every English coronation since 1066 has happened here, on a chair that once held the Stone of Scone
source: Wikimedia Commons: Westminster Abbey (St. Peter) (47537372181).jpg

name: Court of the Lions
blurb: Fountain courtyard of the Alhambra (14th century) · Granada, Spain — its twelve marble lions are one of the rare figurative sculptures in Islamic art, which traditionally avoided depicting animals and people.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Fountain patio de los Leones Alhambra Granada Spain.jpg

name: The Arnolfini Portrait
blurb: Jan van Eyck, 1434 · National Gallery, London — look for the tiny convex mirror on the back wall: it reflects the whole room, including two figures who may be the painter himself.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Van Eyck - Arnolfini Portrait.jpg

name: Aksum
blurb: Towering carved granite stelae of an ancient Ethiopian kingdom, c. 4th century AD — one was looted by Mussolini's Italy in 1937 and only returned, in pieces, by cargo plane in 2005.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Stela in Main Stelae Field - Axum (Aksum) - Ethiopia - 01 (8701108913).jpg

name: Baalbek
blurb: Lebanon's colossal Roman temple complex, 2nd century AD — raised on some of the largest cut stones ever used in construction, including a nearby block weighing close to 1,000 tonnes.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lebanon, Baalbek, Temple of Bacchus.jpg

name: Baths of Caracalla
blurb: Monumental public bathing complex, completed AD 216 · its ruins inspired the grand vaulted halls of New York's original Penn Station and Chicago's Union Station
source: Wikimedia Commons: Baths of Caracalla 2.JPG

name: Belém Tower
blurb: Manueline fortress-tower guarding Lisbon's harbour, early 16th century · one carved gargoyle is a rhinoceros, based on a famous woodcut whose artist never actually saw one
source: Wikimedia Commons: Torre Belém April 2009-4a.jpg

name: Benin Bronzes
blurb: Brass palace plaques of the Kingdom of Benin, 15th–16th century · despite the name, most are brass, cast by lost-wax technique — British forces looted the palace in 1897
source: Wikimedia Commons: At the British Museum 2024 017.jpg

name: Carnac Stones
blurb: Brittany’s miles-long rows of standing stones — the largest gathering of megaliths on Earth, c. 3300 BC
source: Wikimedia Commons: Carnac Standing Stones Alignment, Carnac, Brittany - panoramio.jpg

name: Chan Chan
blurb: The vast adobe capital of the Chimú kingdom on Peru's coast, c. 1400 · the largest adobe city ever built in the Americas — also among the most endangered, in El Niño rains
source: Wikimedia Commons: Vast Abobe Ruins at Chan Chan.JPG

name: Chartres Cathedral
variants: cathedral of our lady of chartres
blurb: Rebuilt after the 1194 fire with its stained glass intact, mainly 12th–13th century · its cobalt 'Chartres blue' stained glass uses a medieval recipe never fully reproduced since
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cathedral Notre Dame, Chartres (3729893669).jpg

name: Codex Sinaiticus
blurb: One of the oldest Bibles in Greek, with a complete New Testament, 4th century AD · its pages are split across four institutions — the Sinai monastery where found disputes how they got there
source: Wikimedia Commons: Codex Sinaiticus Matthew 1,1-2,5.JPG

name: Column of Marcus Aurelius
blurb: Rome's spiralling marble war record — deliberately modelled on Trajan's Column, but starring a very different, much bloodier war, 2nd century AD.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Column of Marcus Aurelius, Rome.jpg

name: Copán
blurb: Maya city in Honduras renowned for its intricately carved stone stelae, c. 700 AD · its Hieroglyphic Stairway carries the longest known Maya inscription — reassembled wrong, order still debated
source: Wikimedia Commons: Copán Maya stelae 2.jpg

name: Cyrus Cylinder
blurb: Clay cylinder in which Cyrus the Great, fresh off conquering Babylon in 539 BC, freed its captives and restored their gods — later hailed as history's first human-rights charter.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Cyrus Cylinder 2.jpg

name: Dead Sea Scrolls
blurb: Discovered in 1947 when a Bedouin shepherd boy threw a rock into a cave and heard something break.
attribution: Photography by Ardon Bar Hama (see [2], author of original document is unknown.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Great Isaiah Scroll Ch53.jpg

name: Diamond Sutra
blurb: Woodblock-printed Buddhist scroll dated 868 AD — the world's earliest complete dated printed book, nearly 600 years before Gutenberg · British Library, London
source: Wikimedia Commons: Diamond Sutra of 868 AD - The Diamond Sutra (868), frontispiece and text - BL Or. 8210-P.2.jpg

name: Elgin Marbles
blurb: c. 447–438 BC · British Museum, London — at the center of a 200-year tug-of-war between Athens and London over whether they belong on the Parthenon.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Part of the central section-East frieze-Elgin Marbles-British Museum.jpg

name: Ghent Altarpiece
blurb: Begun by Hubert van Eyck, completed by his brother Jan in 1432 — the most stolen artwork in history · Ghent, Belgium
attribution: Jan van Eyck (presumably Hubert van Eyck)
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lamgods open.jpg

name: Gutenberg Bible
blurb: First major book printed in Europe with movable type (1455) · about 49 copies survive worldwide
attribution: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress
source: Wikimedia Commons: An illuminated page of the...Gutenberg Bible... LCCN2006680004.jpg

name: Gyeongbokgung
blurb: Seoul's grand royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, first built in 1395 · left in ruins two centuries after invasion, rebuilt in 1867 — Japan then built its HQ right in front
source: Wikimedia Commons: Front view of the Imperial Throne Hall Geunjeongjeon at Gyeongbokgung Palace with blue sky in Seoul.jpg

name: Hampi
blurb: Ruined capital of Vijayanagara and its carved stone chariot, 16th century · European visitors compared it to Rome at its height — sacked so thoroughly in 1565 it was never resettled
source: Wikimedia Commons: Stone Chariot at Vittala temple, Hampi.jpg

name: Hereford Mappa Mundi
blurb: Largest surviving medieval world map on a single sheet, c. 1300 · it places Jerusalem dead-centre, east at the top — real kingdoms mixed with Eden and mythical monsters
source: Wikimedia Commons: Hereford-Karte.jpg

name: Jerash
blurb: Roman provincial city in Jordan and its sweeping oval colonnade, 2nd century AD · its ancient hippodrome still hosts chariot races, re-enacted by actors in Roman legionary costume
source: Wikimedia Commons: Jerash - Oval Forum 02.jpg

name: Great Mosque of Kairouan
blurb: One of Islam's oldest great mosques, in Tunisia, with the world's oldest minaret · its prayer hall is held up by recycled Roman and Byzantine columns of mismatched heights
source: Wikimedia Commons: Courtyard and minaret of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, Tunisia.jpg

name: Kilwa Kisiwani Ruins
blurb: Coral-stone ruins of a Swahili trading sultanate, Great Mosque built from 11th century · Ibn Battuta called it one of the most beautiful cities he'd seen, built on the gold and ivory trade
source: Wikimedia Commons: Great Mosque Kilwa Kisiwani Tanzania.jpg

name: Kizhi Pogost
blurb: Russia's stacked-dome wooden churches on an island in Lake Onega, built without a single nail, 18th century.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Transfiguration Church of Kizhi island.jpg

name: Laocoön and His Sons
blurb: c. 40–30 BC · Vatican Museums, Rome — its 1506 rediscovery in a Roman vineyard was attended by Michelangelo himself, and helped kick off the Renaissance craze for classical sculpture.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Laocoon and His Sons.jpg

name: Las Meninas
blurb: Diego Velázquez, 1656 · Museo del Prado, Madrid — Velázquez painted himself into the scene, brush in hand, working on the very canvas we're looking at.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Las Meninas, by Diego Velázquez, from Prado in Google Earth.jpg

name: Leptis Magna
blurb: Grand Roman city on the Libyan coast, adorned by the emperor Septimius Severus · its grandest buildings were funded by Septimius Severus, born right here, Rome's first African-born emperor
source: Wikimedia Commons: Leptis Magna, Al-Khums, Libya 4.jpg

name: Library of Celsus
blurb: Roman marble library facade at Ephesus, c. 117 AD — Celsus himself is buried in a stone sarcophagus beneath it, making his library also his tomb.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ephesus Celsus Library Façade.jpg

name: Longmen Grottoes
blurb: Chinese cliff carved with thousands of Buddhas, crowned by a colossal Vairocana, 7th century · the colossal Buddha's face is thought to resemble Wu Zetian, China's only female emperor
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ancient Buddhist Grottoes at Longmen- Fengxian Temple, Vairocana Buddha.jpg

name: Shore Temple
blurb: Granite temple standing by the Bay of Bengal at Mahabalipuram, 8th century AD · legend told of six sister temples swallowed by the sea — the 2004 tsunami briefly bared structures offshore
source: Wikimedia Commons: Mamallapuram, Shore Temple, India.jpg

name: Mapungubwe Gold Rhino
blurb: Gold-foil rhinoceros figurine from a royal burial, c. 13th century AD · under apartheid, authorities downplayed research on the wealthy African kingdom that made it
attribution: Sian Tiley-Nel / University of Pretoria Museums
source: Wikimedia Commons: UP rhino.JPG

name: Matsumoto Castle
blurb: Japan's black-walled 'Crow Castle', a 16th-century keep in the Alps · unlike most reconstructed Japanese castles, its wooden keep is largely original, its walls black
source: Wikimedia Commons: 松本城 - Matsumoto Castle - Flickr - tsuruta yosuke.jpg

name: Meroë Pyramids
blurb: Steep royal pyramids of the Kushite kings in Sudan, c. 300 BC–300 AD — there are more pyramids here than in all of Egypt.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Meroe Pyramids - 33110830438.jpg

name: Mesa Verde
blurb: Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings beneath a Colorado canyon rim, 13th century — Cliff Palace is the largest cliff dwelling in North America, abandoned within a generation for reasons still debated.
source: Wikimedia Commons: MesaVerdeNationalParkCliffPalace.jpg

name: Nabta Playa Circle
blurb: Prehistoric megalithic calendar circle, c. 4800 BC · built by cattle-herders in a then-green Sahara, its stones may align to the summer solstice
source: Wikimedia Commons: Calendar aswan.JPG

name: Newgrange
blurb: Ireland's Neolithic passage tomb, carved with spirals and older than Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza alike, c. 3200 BC.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Entrance Stone - Newgrange - Detail.jpg

name: Ollantaytambo
blurb: Inca fortress-town of steep stone terraces in Peru's Sacred Valley, 15th century · the Inca once defeated the Spanish here in battle — nearby, huge 'tired stones' lie where builders left them
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ollantaytambo Inca terraces1.jpg

name: Olympia Stadium
blurb: Stadium of the ancient Games (first held 776 BC); the vaulted entrance is 3rd century BC · athletes at the ancient Games competed naked — married women were banned from watching, on pain of death
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ancient Olympic Stadium Entrance (5987161338).jpg

name: Palenque
blurb: Maya pyramid-tomb rising from the Chiapas jungle — its ruler Pakal's carved sarcophagus lid is the image conspiracy theorists insist shows an ancient astronaut, 7th century AD.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Palenque Temple of Inscriptions.JPG

name: Palmyra
blurb: Roman-era caravan city of Syria — its great arch stood 1,800 years until ISIS dynamited it in 2015
source: Wikimedia Commons: Palmyra - Monumental Arch.jpg

name: Prambanan
blurb: Java's soaring Hindu temple compound of pointed spires, 9th century AD — local legend says it was built in a single night, one temple short of a cursed princess's demand for a thousand.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Shiva Temple of Prambanan in Java Indonesia.jpg

name: Sanchi Stupa
blurb: India's great Buddhist stupa and its carved gateways, begun under Ashoka · its carved gateways never show the Buddha in human form — early art used symbols instead, like a wheel
source: Wikimedia Commons: Stupa 1, Sanchi 02.jpg

name: Shwedagon Pagoda
blurb: Myanmar's great stupa crowning Yangon, plated in tonnes of gold and said to enshrine strands of the Buddha's own hair · its spire is crowned by a golden orb studded with diamonds, including a 76-carat stone at the very tip
source: Wikimedia Commons: Shwedagon Pagoda, Golden stupa, Yangon, Myanmar.jpg

name: Standard of Ur
blurb: Despite the name, nobody actually knows what it was for — Woolley's 'battle standard' theory has since given way to guesses that it's a lyre soundbox or a treasure chest.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Standard of Ur front view.jpg

name: Stone Town Zanzibar Door
blurb: Brass-studded carved wooden door of Swahili-Omani style, 19th century · the brass studs were an Indian design to stop war elephants battering doors — purely decorative by Zanzibar
source: Wikimedia Commons: Detail of Carved Wooden Door - Stone Town - Zanzibar - Tanzania (8841700340).jpg

name: Summer Palace
blurb: Beijing's imperial lakeside garden-palace, rebuilt in the 1880s by the Dowager Empress Cixi — reportedly using funds meant for China's navy.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Summer Palace over Kunming Lake and Nanhu Island.jpg

name: Tara Brooch
blurb: Elaborate Celtic gilt-silver pseudo-penannular brooch, early 8th century AD · despite the name, it has no link to the Hill of Tara — found near a beach, renamed for marketing
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ireland 2010 etc 029.jpg

name: Tassili Rock Art
blurb: Prehistoric painted rock shelters, c. 10,000-1,000 BC · its paintings show a Sahara now unrecognisable — giraffes, hippos and crocodiles thriving centuries ago
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Tanzoumaitak cave painting in Tassili n'ajjer.jpg

name: Pyramid of the Sun
blurb: Colossal stepped pyramid at Teotihuacán, Mexico — the third-largest pyramid on Earth, built c. 200 AD by a civilisation whose own name for itself has been lost to time.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pyramid of the Sun, Teotihuacan, from path to parking lot.jpg

name: Tiwanaku
blurb: Andean ceremonial centre and its carved Gate of the Sun, Bolivia, c. 500 AD · by the time the Inca found these ruins, long abandoned, legend credited a race of giants
source: Wikimedia Commons: Bol-tihuanaco-sonnentor.jpg

name: Trajan's Column
blurb: 113 AD · Trajan's Forum, Rome — Trajan's entire Dacian military campaign spirals up the column in relief; unrolled, the frieze would stretch some 200 metres.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Trajan's Column (48423812647).jpg

name: Trundholm Sun Chariot
blurb: Bronze Age horse-drawn gilded sun disc on wheels, c. 1400 BC · one face of the sun disc is gilded gold, the other plain bronze — day and night journeys
source: Wikimedia Commons: Solvognen DO-6865 2000.jpg

name: Uxmal
blurb: Pyramid of the Magician, built in five phases, 6th–10th century AD · legend says it was built overnight by a magical dwarf hatched from an egg, to explain an unusual pyramid
source: Wikimedia Commons: Pyramid of the Magician (Pirámide del Adivino), Zona Arqueológica de Uxmal, Yucatan, Mexico.jpg

name: Warren Cup
blurb: Its explicit homoerotic relief scenes made it too controversial for the British Museum to put on public display for decades after acquiring it.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Warren Cup - musical instruments.jpg

name: Wawel Castle
blurb: Royal castle on Wawel Hill, mainly 14th-16th century · legend says a dragon lived in the cave below, tricked by a cobbler into eating a sulphur-stuffed sheep
source: Wikimedia Commons: Wawel Castle view from south. Krakow, Poland.jpg

name: Djenne Terracotta
blurb: Hunched terracotta figure from the inland Niger Delta, 13th–15th century · almost all were looted before excavation, so scholars can't agree who they depict or why they're hunched
source: Wikimedia Commons: Seated figure grom Mali, 13th century, Djenné peoples, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1981.218.JPG

name: Gedi Ruins
blurb: Ruined Swahili palace town swallowed by forest, 13th–17th century · Chinese porcelain and Persian glass found here show this Kenyan town's Indian Ocean trade links
source: Wikimedia Commons: Palace at Gedi Ruins.jpg

name: Hope Diamond
blurb: Once part of the French Crown Jewels, stolen during the Revolution — it's trailed a 'curse' legend ever since, with owners said to have met ruin, madness, or the guillotine.
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Hope Diamond - SIA.jpg

name: Ishango Bone
blurb: Notched bone tally tool, c. 20,000 years old · some read its notches as an early lunar calendar; others see arithmetic, even prime numbers
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ishango bone.jpg

name: Kerma Deffufa
blurb: Massive mudbrick temple mound, c. 2500-1500 BC · one of the largest ancient structures in sub-Saharan Africa, built by Kerma, which rivalled Egypt
source: Wikimedia Commons: Kerma-Deffufa.jpg

name: Khami Ruins
blurb: Dry-stone royal capital with decorative walling, 15th-17th century · built as a successor capital after Great Zimbabwe's fall, its walls carry rare checkerboard patterns
source: Wikimedia Commons: Khami Ruins, so-called Monolith Platform.jpg

name: Ziggurat of Ur
blurb: Sumer's stepped brick temple-mountain at Ur, c. 2100 BC — built for the moon god Nanna in the city the Bible names as Abraham's birthplace.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ancient ziggurat at Ali Air Base Iraq 2005.jpg

name: Utrecht Psalter
blurb: Carolingian psalter with vivid pen-sketch illustrations, c. AD 820–835 · its energetic pen sketches were so influential English scribes copied them centuries later
source: Wikimedia Commons: Utrecht Psalter.jpg

name: Winchester Bible
blurb: Largest surviving 12th-century English illuminated bible, c. 1160–1175 · it was never finished — several pages are bare pencil outlines, abandoned mid-illustration
source: Wikimedia Commons: God addressing Jeremiah, Winchester Bible, 1160-75 (22797800517).jpg

name: Terentius Neo and His Wife
variants: portrait of the baker and his wife
blurb: Fresco portrait of a Pompeii baker and his wife, 1st century AD, buried by Vesuvius in 79 · both husband and wife hold writing tools, signalling a rare Roman portrait of shared literacy
source: Wikimedia Commons: MANNapoli 9058 couple painting.jpg
